scenarioStory.history: Grandmother was babysitting and stepped out of the room for approximately 10-15 minutes. She returned to find her grandson sitting on the bathroom floor with her diltiazem bottle open and several loose pills scattered on the floor; she cannot say how many, if any, he actually swallowed. She called 911 immediately. Time since possible ingestion is uncertain, estimated 15-45 minutes.
scenarioStory.course: Initial Contact: Crew arrives to find a 3-year-old male who appears alert and playful, sitting near his grandmother's open diltiazem bottle with several pills unaccounted for. Vital signs are currently near normal for age, but the exact quantity and timing of ingestion are unknown. → History obtained, charcoal and IV access initiated: Crew confirms the ingestion history and timing, identifies the medication as a calcium channel blocker (diltiazem), and since the child remains alert and within the first hour of possible ingestion, administers weight-based activated charcoal and establishes IV access while placing continuous cardiac and pulse oximetry monitoring. → Bradycardia and hypotension develop, calcium given: As predicted for a sustained-release calcium channel blocker ingestion, the child develops delayed-onset symptomatic bradycardia and hypotension. The crew recognizes this, considers atropine per protocol sequence, and administers weight-based calcium gluconate. → Heart rate and perfusion improve, transport: The child's heart rate and blood pressure improve following calcium gluconate and a fluid bolus. He is packaged and transported to a pediatric-capable facility with continuous monitoring, as delayed re-deterioration remains possible with extended-release agents.

patientInformation.patientCondition: Unknown ingestion, found with grandmother's pill bottle

scenarioEvents.name: Initial Contact
scenarioEvents.description: Crew arrives to find a 3-year-old male who appears alert and playful, sitting near his grandmother's open diltiazem bottle with several pills unaccounted for. Vital signs are currently near normal for age, but the exact quantity and timing of ingestion are unknown.
relatedChecklist: Obtain ingestion history: agent, quantity, timing; bring bottle/pills to ED
Attach continuous cardiac monitor and pulse oximetry; establish IV access
Activated charcoal 14 g PO (14 kg x 1 g/kg), given within first hour, airway protected

scenarioEvents.name: History obtained, charcoal and IV access initiated
scenarioEvents.description: Crew confirms the ingestion history and timing, identifies the medication as a calcium channel blocker (diltiazem), and since the child remains alert and within the first hour of possible ingestion, administers weight-based activated charcoal and establishes IV access while placing continuous cardiac and pulse oximetry monitoring.
relatedChecklist: Atropine 0.28 mg IV (14 kg x 0.02 mg/kg; max 0.5 mg), q5min to total 1 mg
Calcium gluconate 840 mg IV over 10 min (14 kg x 60 mg/kg)
IV fluid bolus 280 mL NS (14 kg x 20 mL/kg) for hypoperfusion

scenarioEvents.name: Bradycardia and hypotension develop, calcium given
scenarioEvents.description: As predicted for a sustained-release calcium channel blocker ingestion, the child develops delayed-onset symptomatic bradycardia and hypotension. The crew recognizes this, considers atropine per protocol sequence, and administers weight-based calcium gluconate.
relatedChecklist: Repeat vital signs and ECG frequently en route for delayed re-deterioration
Contact poison control / medical control for ongoing guidance

scenarioEvents.name: Heart rate and perfusion improve, transport
scenarioEvents.description: The child's heart rate and blood pressure improve following calcium gluconate and a fluid bolus. He is packaged and transported to a pediatric-capable facility with continuous monitoring, as delayed re-deterioration remains possible with extended-release agents.

scenarioEvents.name: Charcoal given despite declining mental status
scenarioEvents.description: The crew administers activated charcoal after the child's mental status has already begun to decline, without first protecting the airway. The child vomits and aspirates a portion of the charcoal, causing acute desaturation and coughing.
relatedChecklist: Suction airway, position for airway protection, support oxygenation

scenarioEvents.name: Calcium withheld despite worsening bradycardia
scenarioEvents.description: Without calcium gluconate, the child's bradycardia and hypotension worsen progressively, moving toward refractory shock that will require glucagon and transcutaneous pacing as rescue measures.
relatedChecklist: Glucagon 0.5 mg IV (patient <25 kg), calcium gluconate, consider pacing
